image_description:
## 1. Chart type
- **Horizontal 100% stacked bar chart**

## 2. Layout techniques
- Uses **stacking**: each horizontal bar is split into **Yes** and **No** segments that sum to 100%.
- Uses **grouped spacing** to separate sets of related terms.
- Does **not** use faceting or small multiples.

## 3. Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| Word/term | Categorical/nominal | Row position; text label at left |
| Response category (Yes / No) | Categorical/nominal | Color/hue (green for Yes, pink for No); stacked bar segment |
| Percentage of respondents | Quantitative | Bar length/width along horizontal position; numeric labels inside segments |
| Related term groupings | Categorical/nominal | Vertical grouping/spacing between rows |

comments.raw_comment: What I’ve noticed is that there seems to be a general disuse for words that people have deemed more appropriate or more inclusive. For example a majority of people would not use the term Latinx or AAPI, and they’re a majority who would use BIPOC as well. I wonder what their personal reason is for not using these words. I believe that it is because the people themselves that are apart of these groups don’t like the use of these words to describe them, for example, I don’t know any Latino person who wants to be called Latinx. This affects my community because we are all affect by what other people refer to us as and want our labels to be respected. If I could give this graph a heading it would be “do labels matter?”

comments.raw_comment: My first reaction to this graph was surprise. I think that it is so interesting to see all the different names for one ethnic group that I’ve never heard of before or would never even think to call someone. Through observing this graph, I noticed how the words that were commonly used, were the phrases that I’ve heard spoken the most around me. I was also surprised to see that the acronym phrases, A.A Pi and BIPOC were used a fair bit, being phrases that I have never even heard of before. It's interesting to think about how different words impact other cultures and how it's essential to recognize how certain words are seen as respectful, while others may be derogatory. Talking to others, you should always be mindful of the racial terms you are using to address them, because you don't not know how a certain phrase will affect them. Regarding this,  it is important to acknowledge the cultures of others in my community because we are a very diverse town, filled with many different races of people. Recognizing how certain phrases and words impact those around us, is necessary for a connected and prosperous world.

1) I noticed that some of the traditional terms that are used are being answered with "yes" rather than "no." From this, it's not absurd to assume that majority of people are content without the use of some of these newer terms like "Latinx." Of course, this doesn't mean we should just allow that smaller percentage to be uncomfortable. 
2) I wonder which generations were answering in this survey. As time passed, terms became more acceptable or more understandably offensive. Many older people still use some of these terms, though. When they were younger, those were normal things to say and call people every day and nobody would be bothered. 
3) This relates to me because I'm of very mixed heritages, so I have immersed myself with so many people from different places in my life. My maternal grandmother is native South Korean and she tells me stories from when she was younger and her experiences in Korea. So much has changed since then, including language. 
I would call this graph "What are the proper terms to refer to people with?"

comments.raw_comment:
After looking at this graph, I noticed that many people prefer to use terms that are not older. Terms like BIPOC or AAPI are less popular than terms like Asian or Person of Color which have been around for decades. These people have probably been using these terms for years, and they may be unaware of the new terms and what has become disrespectful. 
This article led me to wonder what people of that descent would prefer to be called. I would like to ask an African American, or Black, person which term they would prefer. I don’t know who was interviewed in this article, so it might be just a bunch of white people. Of course, as a white person, I do not have any say in what terms should or should not be used, but I would like to speak to someone who does to figure out which terms are perceived as offensive and which are inclusive.
I live in the South, which is known for being highly conservative and not very progressive, so I still hear terms that are highly offensive and have been widely avoided. Although many people still use words that are offensive where I live, plenty of people are trying to change the terms they use.
I would name this graph “Offensive or Inclusive?”

comments.raw_comment:
According to the article, the terms “Latinx”, “AAPI”, “BIPOC”, and “Nonwhite” are the 4 least popular terms in the article.
The term Latinx is often criticized as it does not read like a Spanish word whatsoever. ‘Latinx’ as a term was never intended to be used in Spanish, however I still agree with many Latinos that a word derived from Latin-America should be feasibly pronounced in Spanish. Though ‘Latino’ is a masculine adjective, masculine terms in Spanish are often used as a neutral term as well. If a more neutral term is still desired, you can use Latin-American. I’ve also heard ‘e’ be suggested as a gender-neutral suffix in Spanish, which at least makes sense to say out loud. I described myself as Latine for a time while figuring out my gender, and I enjoyed useing the term-- however I can’t really speak for others as I have lived a much whiter life than a Latino one.
The low usage of AAPI is likely caused by a mix of it not being as widely known to most people as other terms, and the fact that it conflates two different ethnic groups.
The term BIPOC has been used to replace the term POC by some, but it is a new term and from what I can tell it has very little difference from POC. Very few people feel the need to change to the new term due to what is often read as redundancy.
I have no comments on the term nonwhite.

Note that I am not a person of color! If I've said anything ignorant or hurtful, please let me know. No explanation needed, unless you want to give one.

comments.raw_comment:
After looking at this graph, and reading the article, I wasn’t too surprised by the results. There is so many different terms used these days to describe people, because no one wants to offend anyone. It’s hard to please everyone with the terms we use, and different people prefer to be called different things. Instead of using one word we think would be best, I think we should ask specific people with what they are comfortable with. For example, lots of people like to be called African American, and that's what I’m used to saying as well. But, sometimes, it’s not the correct term to use. For example, you can be Brazilian or Jamaican, so that term wouldn’t fit. That’s why I think it’s important to ask others instead of basing what we say off of one graph. 
          Some of the terms on this graph I have never even heard before, and if lot’s of people say they say it, I wonder if that's accurate. Are people putting certain responses based off what they think sounds the best?
           In my community, I hear many terms that I would never dare saying. I live in the South, and go to high school, and I hear people say things in the hallways that they would never say to their grandparents. If my school took a survey, offensive terms would have extremely high percentages, which is so very sad. I think it’s best

comments.raw_comment:
1) What do you notice?
I noticed that more encompassing terms are used less than specific ones. Terms like hispanic, asian, or african american were largely used more than latinx, bipoc, or aapi. Furthermore, stating someone's specific background outweighed the use of all the more general phrases such as "people of color" or "non-white," that category having every term be not used by over 50% of Americans. Out of all the terms, Americans would say Hispanic the most (87%) and Latinx the least (22%). 
2) What do you wonder?
I wonder what was the racial demographic of the Americans surveyed, as well as their age range. From my point of view, the terms that seem to be used less in the graph are used more by younger, marginalized people, rather than those who are older and aren't used to certain descriptors.  
3) How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community because amongst my generation there has been a push for more inclusive language, which as seen by the graph consists of the terms being used the least.
4) What’s going on in this graph?
This graph shows different words, and the percent of Americans that would or would not say them. My headline would be "Identifiers, Which ones are Americans Using?"

comments.raw_comment:
What I first noticed about this graph is that the first word of each graph is what I would assume is the most baseline way to refer to someone of color. I myself am Hispanic and I have only overheard the word "Latinx" less than three times in my life. I don't know exactly what it means, if it is different from Hispanic or Latino. Whenever I have been referred to as Latinx I haven't felt insulted or disrespected. 
This relates to my community because there are several things that my Hispanic family and friends would feel insulted if someone used specific words to allude our Mexican heritage. I always thought and still do think that Hispanic is the most respectful way to refer to someone of Mexican heritage. I cannot speak my opinion for any other of these graphs because I am Hispanic so I don't know how any other person about their heritage personally feels.
But, I have always mentioned people from Asia or have heritage from Asia as Asians. And people of darker skin color as African American. Because that is what I always believed was to be the most respectful way to say it.
This graph is just showing what the majority of American Adults refer to people of different heritage. I have always believed that there is no need to call anyone by these names unless it is asked. I would never bluntly call someone by one of these names, I would always just call them by their name. I just don't feel that it is needed because we are all just human beings.

comments.raw_comment: Looking at the graph I see the different terms people have started using to describe other people, I have at least heard all of these terms once, I've seen some others used more online than in person and some “main '' others that are used in real life in the south where I live. I wonder if some of the terms people use are because they believe it makes them “woke” and what other people use only because it's the only term they know and were taught and grew up with. I would also like to see a graph of what the ages are and the age gaps between what the older generation uses and the younger generation uses, what they think of each term and how they feel about it. I don’t think I can have a say in this as a cisgender white person in the south, this isn’t my community or my ground to say what terms are “better than others” each term has its own history and can be important to some people and unimportant to others it all comes down to perspective. I think the article name “Terms of the U.S and what they mean to you”

comments.raw_comment:
To me, this graph speaks volumes on what society is and how we have decided to combat racism. I replied to another New York Times article on an issue of racism and how a mural in a Law School is under the decision of removal after many onlookers felt uncomfortable with its art style and its portrayal of slavery. My opinion was that the ones who should decide what should happen with the mural should be the same people who were affected by what the mural depicts. Personally, being Caucasian, I don’t experience racism as someone of color or race would and I'm not as affected by it but I can try to give my voice of reason.
  In this day and age people forget what can be offensive and try to stick on the side that likely has no negative connotations. Calling someone “black” or “asian” to some 20% of people is not a term they would use but to the majority, these terms aren’t racist and rather are just a descriptive feature that is provided when they look at someone. Similar to what I said in my comment on the mural, I believe that the people who decide whether a term is offensive or not should be decided by the group that is going to be called or referred to by those terms.

The name of this graph though, could be improved. comments.raw_comment:
This chart has terms such as “Latinx” and “BIPOC” which I've heard rarely and don’t necessarily know what they stand for. And after researching them they seem to be very inclusive but fairly new. Not many people in my area refer to others using “Latinx”, “BIPOC”, or “A.A.I.P” and usually stick to the more vague terms such as  “Asian” or “Hispanic”. I can see why they aren’t very popular in this study of about 4,500 people with “no” percentages of 78% for Latinx and 70% for BIPOC, likely because as I stated above, they are generally newer terms coming out in the 2000s. It makes sense that newer terms, especially related to race and ethnicity, are not used in order to avoid offending others because the meaning has not yet been globalized. While everyone can do a quick google search, just as I did, many people don’t care to look or even know to look, thus resulting in a large population that doesn’t understand the terms used above. This is why some of the most popular terms are “Hispanic” or “Asian” when asked if Americans use certain terms when referring to race and ethnicity. Even though they are pretty vague, most people don’t know any better. It’s obvious that the longer a word is around for, the more widely accepted it's going to be in contrast to newer terms.

What do you notice?
I noticed from the graph that the Americans who responded to this survey decided to say more simple words instead of complex identity words. For example, 81% of Americans are okay with referring to people as Asians, but when it comes to more inclusive terms like A. A. P. I, only 27% say yes to using the term. The same thing goes for the 75% of Americans who say black people compared to 30% who don't say B.I.P.O.C. I noticed this in the graph for the term Latinx, which is more inclusive towards people, yet Americans prefer saying Latino/Latina.

What do you wonder?
I wonder how the results of the graph would differ if a different group of people were interviewed. Do these types of results only vary so much because it's Americans or do all groups of people think this way? Do the results look like this because we're still waiting for these terms to gain popularity? Or is it a thing of racism?

How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community and me because I fall under the Hispanic, Latino/Latina, and Latinx categories, and it is very interesting to see what people prefer to call groups with ethnic backgrounds. This also informs me of what Americans refer to me and my community as.

comments.raw_comment:
This graph is showing the result of what 4,423 Americans refer to people of different races or ethnicities as. I first noticed Americans are very comfortable using the terms “Hispanic and Asian”. Yet Americans rarely use the terms “BIPOC or A.A.P.I”. I wonder why people are more comfortable saying Hispanic or Asian, maybe because they wanted to be “with the crowd”. I’m not sure if there’s a specific reason why people don’t use the specific terms but they’ll use the overall “popular” ethnicity names. I mean this could be to avoid awkward conversations or situations by calling someone the wrong ethnicity, but I do think you could just ask what they would prefer to be called in general. 
  I also wonder in this survey what the ratio of people of different ethnicities to white was. I think this survey could be biased or unreliable information if the ratio wasn’t close to equal. I think they should have done a counter survey to see which terms people of different ethnicities would prefer to be called. With that kind of information we could see the differences and make comments about how they differ and which terms are more comfortable for a person of different ethnicity. I do think using general terms to someone of different ethnicity could be disrespectful in some situations, because if someone is not the ethnicity you assumed, you just called them something they weren’t and that's disrespectful. That's why I always ask what someone would prefer to be called before I assume.

I don’t understand why people have to get all offended and flip out when I genuinely don’t understand the difference between Hispanic and Latino. I mean shouldn’t you be proud of your heritage and excited to teach someone something new. I think in these heated conversations we should start using them as a teaching moment rather than making one feel less of themselves for not knowing something they weren’t taught. 
   Seeing that more people use the word Hispanic than Latinx is because of the fear of being perceived as insensitive. I can understand one not saying Latinx because they don’t fully know what it means and are fearful of being hammered for being incorrect. Personally I think it’s sad that folks are just afraid to be politically incorrect choosing the phrase people of color rather than nonwhite. I mean can’t we just offer each other grace. Not everyone has grown up in a household where they talk about diversity, its beauty and what is/isn’t offensive.

comments.raw_comment:
In this graph, I see that our society has become hyper focused on labeling each other and fitting into specific groups. Although this graph is about race, an age-old concept, many of the terms didn’t exist until now and are just starting to be used more often. As the world has become more culturally and racially inclusive, we have also realized that maybe some of these phrases are too wide-ranging. Although the newer terms, such as “Latinx” and “BIPOC” haven’t gained a ton of popularity yet, they are starting to catch on. I think this is a good thing for the world because it emphasizes smaller groups within larger ethnic groups. Some of these people may have previously been underrepresented and giving them a specific name can help give them the recognition that they deserve. I also think that sometimes people will use the broader terms, like “Asian” or “Hispanic” at times when it may be more appropriate to use a more particular term. I have noticed at school or around town, people who use these broader terms tend to generalize a group of people, sometimes even stereotype them.

comments.raw_comment: The first thing I notice when I look at this graph is how many people don’t like the term “Latinx”. I’d never heard of it before and it made me wonder why people seem to dislike it so much. I understand the context behind why it was made, to be a gender neutral alternative to Latino/Latina, and I guess since nonbinary people are a minority it would make sense why most people prefer not to use it. It reminded me of the term “Womxn” which was made as a gender neutral alternative to the word “Woman” but isn’t nearly as inclusive as people act like it is. Although it claims to be more inclusive of trans women, the label just treats them like they’re not real women by making a specific term to separate them from other women. This reminded me of how, in my community (LGBTQ+), there’s often a lot of controversy about what labels or pride flags are outdated and appropriate to use. For example, the progress pride flag was made to highlight trans and POC queer people, but some people don’t like that they’re highlighted in that design because it makes it seem like they weren’t included in the original rainbow flag. The trend I notice on this graph is that most people prefer more general terms like “Asian” rather than “A.A.P.I.” probably because the newer terms that are made to be more inclusive tend to make the people they’re trying to include only feel more isolated. I would probably title this graph “Preferred Racial Terminology of 2023”.

It was also interesting to note that many Americans used terms such as Hispanic, African American, and Asian when referring to people of color.

The graph's significance lies in its reflection of the language and attitudes of Americans as a collective group. Depending on one's race, ethnicity, or gender, they may be more or less likely to use certain words. 
Moreover, the graph is relevant to individuals interested in promoting diversity, equity, and inclusion, as it sheds light on language habits and preferences of different demographic groups. 
Some questions that the graph may provoke include the factors that influence people's language choices, why certain terms are more common than others, and how language use reflects cultural and social changes over time. By analyzing the data, one can gain insights into language patterns among different communities and raise questions about the inclusiveness of language use in their own community.

comments.raw_comment:
Hispanic, Asian, African American, and Person of Color. What these terms all have in common is that they are broad, umbrella terms used to describe people of varying ethnicities. What I inferred from this graph is that people use terms that make them feel the most comfortable to avoid offending others. However, I don’t think we should focus on what makes us comfortable, and instead use the term that the people who are of these ethnicities identify with. 
When the Black Lives Matter movement first gained momentum, I remember hearing the broad terms in the news, but I also remember seeing interviews and articles talking about “which term is the best” and “which terms are offensive”. People debating if POC was offensive or not, or which terms included which ethnicities. Beyond that, we put so much energy into arguing over these characterizations when we should be focusing on equality and respecting others regardless of their ethnicity instead.

1. I notice that the graphs key specifically says that the question is being asked to Americans. I also notice that the options are split up by racial/ethnic group and that the least favored option by ethnic group is the last term.

2. To build off of my notice I wonder what were the ethnic and racial groups of the Americans being asked as well as the backgrounds of those Americans. Since I'm Hispanic(of a spanish speaking country) ethnically and of African descent racially, I have differing opinions to other people who may be exclusively one or the other, personally I have no issue with the term Latino/Latina, or Black, but from what I have been told by my community, peers, and elders is that terms like "Latinx" or "African American" can be seen as offensive due to the way it clashes with culture. I was told that not all people of African Descent are American, (referring to "Afro-caribbeans") and that "Latinx" does not fit into the spanish language, as the spanish language is "built on gendered words." These are explanations I have found from a varying amount of people, and it doesn't even scratch the surface.

4. What would you say?

comments.raw_comment:
In the chart, I notice people are more comfortable using "umbrella terms" than more specific terms and labels. Using more specific terms like Latinx and Asian American can be good but I think you should know some of the person's background before referring to their label. For example, Latino/Latina are referring to people from Latin America so it would be incorrect to refer to someone from Spain as Latino. The more correct term would be Hispanic. 
    I wonder if people were already more familiar with these terms the statistics would be different. If people correctly educated themselves on these titles then people could correctly refer to a group of people, instead of incorrectly labeling them. It would help make groups more diverse instead of generalizing. For instance, it would be incorrect to say every black person was African American because not every black person has descent from Africa. Many people have descent and traditions from Brazil, Haiti, Columbia, etc.
     Even though there is a big white population at my school, there are still many POC and my area can be very diverse. People should learn about how to refer to groups of people because it can make people feel more comfortable since POC groups seem to be smaller around me. A good way to title this graph could be "Educate your way of speech".

While looking at this graph, something that catches my attention is how spread out peoples choice of words are. Though 4,423 people isn't a huge amount, it gives me a lot of perspectives of how many address race. I definitely see how careless it can be to call someone "nonwhite" or "Black", not only because you might not know their ethnicity, but because how antique those words are. I say antique because those words are truly outdated, and wouldn't be a regular thing to call someone.
          I do believe that it's very important to find out what a person is comfortable with being called, because ethnicity and race are two different things. I can see that the surveyed group who used terms like "nonwhite" might have been influenced wrongly from their parents or media. I also see that a huge percentage of the surveyed group are most comfortable with terms like "Hispanic" and "Asian", which are also common terms I hear around my community.
           Research is an important tool to use if you are in the topic of race and ethnicity. You never know how calling someone one of these terms can effect how you are viewed. This might be why some of the people surveyed used terms such as "BIPOC" and "AAPI". It could be because they might be afraid to use a wrong term, or because they prefer to use a newer and thoughtful term. Overall, this article shows me a a list of terms that people think are more valuable to be heard by an audience of people with mixed ethnicity and race.

comments.raw_comment: There is always a reason behind every graph or statistic, and I think the reason for why the words like “nonwhite”, “BIPOC”, “A.A.P.I”, and “Latinx” are statistically less used is that they are less traditional terms for groups of people, and the main people who use them more than likely inhabit the hyper politically correct sector of humans. For example, according to the Journal of Hispanic Higher Education, the first instance of the term Latinx in academic literature was in 2013. This means that the word has not really had much time to catch on to the general populace. Another example would be the term A.A.P.I, which I had never heard of. This term was first introduced in the 80s, so is much newer than most of the other terms like Asian American, or Asian. I would guess that the older the term, the more popular it is, and vice versa with younger terms. The main thing I do not understand about this graph is the percentage of people that would not say anything about anyone's race. I would have to guess that they would claim to not see color and so they have nothing to say about it, but I cannot be sure. Personally, most of the people I know (including me) use the most popular term for each category and there does not seem to be much fuss among us, but there will always be a person that wants to change things up. If I had to come up with a headline for this graph, it would be something along the lines of “Majority of Americans prefer to use terms that are older, study shows.”

Looking at the graph, I see that there are some people who use all the terms that are listed. Also what I see is that the terms that are the most used are the terms that I see to be least offensive but I can't say anything because I am not a part of any of the mentioned groups.

     Lastly, I thought who in my life calls this group this term or that term. Everyone I have heard reference the first group, I have heard them call them Hispanic and for the second group Asians, for the third, African American, and fourth, person of color. It got me thinking why. Do people use the term they think least offensive or do people use the word they were thought to use. If I were to make the graph, I would call it, "What would you say?".

There were many, many great headlines for this graph.  Our appreciation for all that were submitted. Here are only a few:

“As Language Evolves, Americans Weigh In on Words to Describe Race and Ethnicity” by Lainie of Kentucky; “Woke or Broke?: Will Politically Correct Lingo Catch On?” by Clara of Georgetown Visitation Preparatory School; "Words Americans Use When Talking about Identity" by Metropolitan Montessori Middle School in New York City; “Call Me by My Name” by Ashley of Florida; two from Perth Amboy High School in New Jersey – “A New Generation of Terms: Which Do You Identify With?” by Ashley and “Censorship or Respect: Is Terminology Affecting the Way We See Each Other?” by Samuel, and two from Eaglecrest High School in Aurora, Colorado – “What Will America Call Me Today?” by Temsalet and “America Speaks: Words Americans Would and Wouldn't Say” by Ciaran.

There is no graph for next week.  The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, March 17 with moderation on Wednesday, March 29.  The topic – the Anthropocene.  
 
Signing off – Sharon Hessney from Boston, who uses words like most Baby Boomers (habits die hard), and Sara Stoudt, assistant professor of math at Bucknell in Lewisburg, Pennsylvania, who as a statistician knows that word choice really does matter.

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice
I notice that out of all of the terms used, Latinx is used the least with 22% of the people asked saying they use the term. In contrast, the most agreed upon term is Hispanic with 87% of the people asked saying they use it. It seems that most of the Americans that were questioned stick to more of the older sayings such as Hispanic, Asian/Asian American, and Black/African American and are much less familiar and/or uncomfortable with using the other terms, given the percentages of each of the terms.


What do you wonder?
I wonder why Latino/Latina is used by less of the people asked than Hispanic is considering they’re almost the same and the only difference is the assigning of the masculine and feminine in the words. I’ve also never heard of A.A.P.I. or BIPOC and after doing some research I found that they mean “Asian American/Pacific Islander” and “Black Indigenous Person of Color” respectively. I wonder if the Americans said they didn’t use those terms because they haven’t heard of it like me, or if it’s due to something else.


How does this relate to you and your community?
This relates to my community and I because there are people that come from many different backgrounds in my town and more specifically in my school. And seeing what other people are okay and not okay with saying can be insightful to avoid referring to someone as something they may find offensive.

comments.raw_comment:
1)Due to tradition, people are more prone to employ terms that they are familiar with and at ease with. In lieu of being accurate and respectful, it is simpler to refer to someone by their conventional name. I believe that the older terminology is still in use since it is clearer and simpler. Although insulting, the terms "Asian", "Black", and "Hispanic" are far simpler to remember and pronounce than "A.A.P.I", "latinX", and "BIPOC".
2)I'm curious how long it will take for the more recent, precise terminology to become commonplace. If they are used frequently enough, they will eventually overtake the current descriptive phrases and cease to exist. I'm curious as to why "Black American" is the only politically correct phrase that has more usage than its opposite.
3). I would argue that this refers to my community as well as this generation in general since it is getting more objectionable to use terms that were not offensive ten years ago. There is a significant contrast between the terms that some people would say that would be thought to be non-offensive and the language that many people would use that would today be considered to be offensive, especially living in a more progressive area but remaining in the south.
4)Be careful what you say—what will be considered suitable or offensive?

1. What did I notice? comments.raw_comment: I notice that the graph shows there is a majority of Americans that prefer to use general, basic terms to describe people of different ethnicity groups. For example, 87% of people would say to use the term “Hispanic” while only 22% would use “Latinx.” I wonder if the race and gender of those surveyed affects the words people would and wouldn’t say? I also notice that in the first three categories there is more comfortability in saying certain words for most Americans. For example, 81% would say “Asian.” However, the last category had more “no” than “yes.” 51% say they would not use the term “person of color.” 62% say they would not use the term “nonwhite.” 70% would not use the term “BIPOC.” I wonder why they are not comfortable using the term person of color, but more comfortable using specific terms to describe ethnicities and races? How do people of different races and ethnicities prefer to be labeled as? This affects me because I am definitely cautious and conscientious of not offending people by calling them an offensive term or one that I am unfamiliar with. My headline is “To Say or Not to Say: Terms Americas Would and Would Not Say”

comments.raw_comment: This graph showcases the likelihood of 4,423 Americans using different words.  One of the main things that stands out to me is how the bottom set of graphs have lower percentages of people using them in their vocabulary.  This is most likely because a term like "nonwhite" has a negative connotation and is not the most respectful.  On the other hand, 77% of people say they use the term "African American" and 69% use "Asian American."  These words are not only specific, but they also encourage inclusion.  The term with the highest percentage of use is "Hispanic" with only 13% saying they would not use the word.  I wonder what the demographics of this poll was.  How old were these people?  Do they include themselves as members of the African American, Hispanic, or Asian American communities?  Why do people chose not to use certain terms?  This relates to me and my community because it is important to use respectful terminology to ensure people feel included and valued.  I would entitle this graph: "Would You Say This?"

comments.raw_comment:
Welcome to Wednesday's live moderation of “What’s Going On in This Graph?”  

Today’s graphs are about what proportion of Americans use specific words to describe some ethnicities and races.  The results come from an online survey of 4,423 adults in December 2022. The survey was weighted on gender, age, race, education and region, with a margin of error of plus or minus 1 percentage point. Word choice is extremely contextual, so they asked people simply if they used a term, not whether they preferred one term over another.

From 9 am – 2 pm E.T. today, share with us your responses online for the four questions.  By Friday morning, we’ll reveal the free link to the online article that included these graphs.  
You can get a link to your response to share with your teacher and classmates by clicking the response box below your response “Email me when my comment is published.”  

The next “What’s Going On In This Graph?” will be released by Friday, March 17 with moderation on Wednesday, March 29.  The topic – the Anthropocene!

1. What do you notice?
I notice that there are 11 multiple-variable bar charts, each making up 100% of the sample (4,423 Americans). Each bar refers to a term and indicates whether a person uses it or does not use it based on the variables "yes" and "no." Based on the visual, a majority of the sample uses the terms "Hispanic", "Asian", and "African American."


2. What do you wonder?

I am curious to know what the backgrounds of the people who were surveyed are. Factors, such as age, education, and race, could play a significant role in which terminologies are more commonly used than others.


3. What impact does this have on you and your community?

People in my community use some of these terms when addressing. This visual is definitely impactful since it indicates what might seem appropriate to say and what might seem offensive to say.



4. What's going on in this graph? Write a catchy headline that captures the graph's main idea.

According to the graph, terms such as "Latinx", "A.A.P.I", "BIPOC", and "Nonwhite" are not commonly used by the Americans surveyed. Less than 40% of the sample use these terms, which might indicate that they might sound offensive to someone. On the other hand, the terms "Hispanic", "Asian", and "African American" are commonly used. More than 75% of the sample use these terms.

comments.raw_comment:
What do you notice?
Latinx, A.A.P.I., and BIPOC are the labels most rarely used by Americans. Hispanic, Asian, African American and Person of Color are the most often used words. The least used and most recent comment on the list is Latinx, which refers to all Hispanics. The words with the lowest popularity on the graph are more contemporary expressions that have gained popularity due to racial strife and the expansion of social media. 

What do you wonder?
In what ways are terms like Latinx, A.A.P.I., and BIPOC more inclusive for groups who feel they should be referred to in this way? I'm curious where other terminologies like these comes from. Is there a rise in the use of gender-neutral language as society moves closer to a more accepting culture of all genders, nationalities, and other characteristics?

How does this relate to you and your community?
This applies to my community because there are numerous races represented in my high school, but I was unaware that only a few phrases were used to describe them. For instance, I hear the terms "Hispanic" and "Mexican" much more frequently than terms like "Latino" or a description of the sort of Latino. In contrast, I only hear the word "Black" at our school, where there are hundreds of different students of African heritage. It appears that only generic terminology and a very small number of other words or races are recognized. 

What is going on in the graph?

comments.raw_comment:
Americans: Race Words, Are they "Okay" to Say
I notice that 87% of Americans would say the word "Hispanic" whereas only 22% would say "Latinx". It appears that within races, there is always a word people prefer to say over others. This can also be seen in the Asian race with "Asian" at 81% and "A.A.P.I" at 27%. I wonder why people aren't more inclusive on phrases and words as they begin to become more prevalent in our lives. The words "Person of color" and "BIPOC" are brought up more and more throughout our daily lives, yet less than 50% would use those words. I don't understand why because they aren't harmful words, etc. This relates to my community because in my high school we have hundreds of different races, but I never noticed there were only select words used. For example, I hear "Hispanic" or "Mexican" a lot more than other words like "Latino" or specifying the type of latino. On the other hand, there are hundred of different kids of African descent at our school, and all I hear is "Black". It seems like there are just very few recognition of other words or races and only generalized terms. This graph shows the percent of Americans who say or don't say specific "race words".

comments.raw_comment:
1. Americans are least likely to use the terms Latinx, A.A.P.I., and BIPOC. The most common words are Hispanic, Asian, African American, and Person of Color. Latinx, which is intended to include all Latinos, is the least frequently used and newest word in the list. The least popular words on the graph are more recent expressions that have gained attention due to racial unrest and the growth of social media. This could explain why other terms are more commonly used than these ones, particularly the way America defines races and ethnicities.

2. Why aren't the most inclusive words used more frequently? Is this because the terms are still so new and the majority of people still don't understand them? A.A.P.I. is also much less common than the more straightforward term Asian, whereas both black terms for black people are much closer to what Americans would say when compared to any other race. Maybe because there are as many black Americans as there are white Americans.

3. In relation to my community, I can also understand why some of the terms selected are used more frequently than others. Being Latina, I could also comprehend why the term "Latinx" isn't used more often. This is because it is the most recent and, in my opinion, is not as necessary as people think since the term "Latino," despite being a masculine word, can be used broadly to describe anyone of Latin ancestry.

4. "POC or BIPOC? Preferred Racial Terms by Americans"
